analysis.one_liner: Strips the National Labor Relations Board of its power to enforce federal labor law against employers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have removed the main government enforcer of private-sector labor law, never left the Senate committee it was sent to and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so the National Labor Relations Board could only investigate complaints, not prosecute them, issue binding rules, order violators to stop, or ask federal courts to enforce its decisions. Instead, a worker or union that says an employer broke the law would have to file their own lawsuit in federal court. The board's rulemaking would be limited to its own internal procedures, so it could no longer set rules on things like union elections. The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor issues and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who face union organizing drives or unfair labor practice charges. Today, the board's General Counsel investigates and prosecutes those cases at government expense, and the board can order companies to stop illegal conduct and go to court to enforce its orders. Under this bill, that government enforcement machinery would disappear, and employers would face only private lawsuits brought by individual workers or unions who could afford to litigate.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the General Counsel's authority to issue and prosecute unfair labor practice complaints before the board, leaving only investigation [S2][S3].
It removes the board's authority to prevent unfair labor practices, limiting it to investigating allegations, and repeals its power to ask courts to enforce its orders or seek injunctions [S2][S3].

It bars the board from issuing any rules affecting the substantive or procedural rights of employers, employees, or unions — including rules on unfair labor practices and representation elections — and requires a review and revision or rescission of existing board regulations within six months [S2][S3].

In place of board prosecution, it lets the aggrieved person bring a civil action, including for an injunction, in the federal district court where the violation occurred or in the D.C. federal court [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and unions who rely on the National Labor Relations Board to pursue complaints against employers at no cost to them. Private litigation is expensive and slow, and individual employees illegally fired or threatened for union activity would have to fund their own lawsuits against employers with far greater resources. The board's ability to set uniform election rules would also end, leaving union election procedures less clearly defined.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and unions using labor law protections

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection supporters raise is that the current system lets the board's General Counsel act as both prosecutor and judge over the same case, and this bill is presented as restoring a court-style process where an aggrieved person can seek relief directly in federal court [S2][S3].

The cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge: shifting enforcement from a government prosecutor to private lawsuits puts the burden on individual workers and unions, who rarely have the money to litigate against an employer, so many violations of the National Labor Relations Act would likely go unpunished [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For employers, the bill removes an enforcer and a rulemaker they view as hostile; for workers, it replaces free government enforcement of labor law with a do-it-yourself court system that few individuals can afford, making the law much harder to use in practice. The trade is straightforward: employer relief paid for with worker access to enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on October 24, 2019, joined by five Republican cosponsors: Sens. Cotton, Paul, Blackburn, Cruz, and Rubio [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the National Labor Relations Board kept its authority to prosecute unfair labor practices, issue rules, and enforce orders in court — so workers and unions are no worse off, while employers who would have gained from weaker enforcement gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers and unions, because the bill never advanced

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the National Labor Relations Board of its complaint-prosecution, rulemaking, and enforcement powers.

for.name: Sens. Cotton, Paul, Blackburn, Cruz, and Rubio

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action — no hearing or markup — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support recorded, and the bill never reached a vote where cross-party positions could have shown.

industries.industry: Employers, especially those contesting union organizing
industries.note: The bill removes government prosecution of unfair labor practice charges, board orders, court enforcement, and board rulemaking on elections — leaving employers to face only private lawsuits from workers or unions who can afford to sue. Workers would lose the free enforcement channel they use today.

Unions depend on the board's General Counsel to prosecute employer violations and on board rules governing representation elections; both would be stripped, leaving unions to litigate on their own dime.
Replacing agency prosecution with private civil actions shifts disputes into federal court, where employers and aggrieved workers would both need litigation counsel.
